items.title: National Income Aggregates — GDP, GNP, NNP, NDP, NI
items.body:
**In one line:** National income is the total money value of all final goods and services an economy produces in a year, and GDP, GNP, NNP and NI are just that total measured from slightly different angles.

**Why it is asked:** It is the single most important number in economics — it measures the size of the economy, its growth and (roughly) living standards — and APPSC regularly tests the exact difference between the aggregates and how to convert one into another.

## What the terms mean

- **Final goods and services** = things bought for final use, not for resale or further processing (a loaf of bread you eat, not the flour the baker buys). Counting only final goods avoids **double counting**.
- **GDP (Gross Domestic Product)** = value produced **inside a country's borders**, by residents and foreigners alike.
- **GNP (Gross National Product)** = value produced by a country's **residents/nationals**, wherever in the world they earn it.
- **NFIA (Net Factor Income from Abroad)** = income residents earn abroad minus income foreigners earn here.
- **Depreciation (consumption of fixed capital)** = the wear and tear that uses up machines and buildings during the year.

## The core aggregates

| Aggregate | What it covers | Formula |
|---|---|---|
| GDP | Output within the country's borders (residents + foreigners) | Sum of value added by all sectors |
| GNP | Output by the country's residents anywhere | GDP + NFIA |
| NDP | GDP after setting aside wear and tear | GDP − Depreciation |
| NNP | GNP after setting aside wear and tear | GNP − Depreciation |
| NI | Income actually earned by the factors of production | NNP at Factor Cost |

## Why the formulae work

Think of three small knobs that turn one aggregate into another:
- **Domestic to National:** add **NFIA**, because GNP counts our people's foreign earnings but drops foreigners' earnings here. GDP + NFIA = GNP.
- **Gross to Net:** subtract **Depreciation**, because some output merely replaces worn-out capital and is not a true addition to wealth.
- **Market Price to Factor Cost:** **Factor Cost = Market Price − Indirect Taxes + Subsidies**. Market price is what the buyer pays; factor cost is what producers actually receive once the government's taxes are removed and its subsidies added back.

## How to compute any aggregate (steps)

1. Start from **GDP at market price**.
2. Add **NFIA** to reach **GNP** (or do nothing to stay 'domestic').
3. Subtract **Depreciation** to turn any 'Gross' figure into its 'Net' version.
4. Subtract **Indirect Taxes** and add **Subsidies** to turn 'Market Price' into 'Factor Cost'.
5. **NNP at Factor Cost is National Income.**

## Worked example 1 (easy)

GDP at market price = ₹200 crore and NFIA = +₹10 crore. Find GNP.
- GNP = GDP + NFIA = 200 + 10 = **₹210 crore**. The extra ₹10 crore is what residents earned abroad over what foreigners earned here.

## Worked example 2 (exam level)

Given (₹ crore): GDP at market price = 200, NFIA = −10, Depreciation = 25, Indirect Taxes = 30, Subsidies = 5. Find GNP, NNP and National Income.
- GNP at market price = GDP + NFIA = 200 + (−10) = **190** (NFIA is negative, so GNP is below GDP).
- NNP at market price = GNP − Depreciation = 190 − 25 = **165**.
- National Income = NNP at factor cost = NNP at market price − Indirect Taxes + Subsidies = 165 − 30 + 5 = **₹140 crore**.
- Check: 200 − 10 − 25 − 30 + 5 = 140. ✓

## Common traps

- Adding depreciation instead of subtracting it (depreciation always makes a figure smaller).
- Treating NFIA as always positive — for India it is usually **negative**, so GNP is a little below GDP.
- For factor cost, people reverse the signs: it is **minus taxes, plus subsidies**, not the other way round.

## Don't confuse

**GDP vs GNP:** GDP is about **location** (produced inside India); GNP is about **ownership** (produced by Indians anywhere). The bridge between them is NFIA.

| Who earns it, where | In India's GDP? | In India's GNP? |
|---|---|---|
| A foreign-owned firm producing inside India | Yes (inside the border) | No |
| An Indian company operating abroad | No | Yes — it is part of India's GNP but not its GDP |

## Worked example 3 (net national product)

GDP = ₹500, Depreciation = ₹40, NFIA = +₹15. Find NNP.
- Step 1 (domestic → national): GNP = 500 + 15 = **₹515**.
- Step 2 (gross → net): NNP = 515 − 40 = **₹475**.
- Trap: 500 − 40 = 460 is NDP, not NNP — it forgets NFIA.

## Derived household aggregates

- **Personal Income (PI)** = income actually received by households, including transfers like pensions.
- **Disposable Income (DI)** = PI − direct (personal) taxes = what households can spend or save.

### In short

**The story in brief.** The background, the cause-and-effect and every term used are explained in the sections above; the essential facts to carry into the exam are these.

**TL;DR**

- GDP = output within a country's borders (residents + foreigners); GNP = output by a country's residents anywhere = GDP + NFIA.
- NDP = GDP − Depreciation; NNP = GNP − Depreciation.
- National Income (NI) = NNP at Factor Cost.
- Factor Cost = Market Price − Indirect Taxes + Subsidies.
- Disposable Income = Personal Income − direct taxes.
- GDP is about location (inside the border); GNP is about ownership (by residents) — the bridge is NFIA.
keyPoints: GDP = output within a country's borders (residents + foreigners); GNP = output by a country's residents anywhere = GDP + NFIA.
NDP = GDP − Depreciation; NNP = GNP − Depreciation.
National Income (NI) = NNP at Factor Cost.
Factor Cost = Market Price − Indirect Taxes + Subsidies.
Disposable Income = Personal Income − direct taxes.
GDP is about location (inside the border); GNP is about ownership (by residents) — the bridge is NFIA.

items.title: Nominal vs Real GDP & the GDP Deflator
items.body:
**In one line:** Nominal GDP values output at this year's prices, real GDP values the same output at a fixed base-year's prices, and the GDP deflator is the ratio that measures how much of the rise in nominal GDP is just higher prices.

**Why it is asked:** Growth is only meaningful in real terms, and the deflator is the broadest inflation measure in the economy; examiners test whether you can separate 'more output' from 'higher prices'.

## What the terms mean

- **Nominal (money) GDP** = output valued at **current-year market prices**. It rises when output rises and also when prices rise, so on its own it overstates real growth.
- **Real GDP** = output valued at **constant base-year prices**. By freezing prices it shows the **true change in the quantity** of goods and services.
- **GDP deflator** = a price index covering **every** good and service in GDP.

## Why it works

Nominal GDP = quantities × current prices; real GDP = quantities × base-year prices. Dividing one by the other cancels the quantities and leaves only the price change — which is exactly what a price index should capture.

## How to use it (steps)

1. GDP Deflator = (Nominal GDP ÷ Real GDP) × 100.
2. A deflator above 100 means prices have risen since the base year; in the base year itself nominal = real, so the deflator is exactly 100.
3. Real growth rate = percentage change in **real** GDP between two years.

## Worked example 1 (easy)

Nominal GDP = ₹500 crore, Real GDP = ₹400 crore.
- Deflator = (500 ÷ 400) × 100 = **125**. Prices are 25% higher than in the base year.

## Worked example 2 (exam level)

Base year: nominal = real = ₹1,000 crore. Next year: nominal GDP = ₹1,320 crore, real GDP = ₹1,100 crore.
- Deflator = (1,320 ÷ 1,100) × 100 = **120**, so prices rose 20%.
- Real growth = (1,100 − 1,000) ÷ 1,000 × 100 = **10%**.
- Note the nominal figure rose 32%, but only 10% of that is extra output; the rest is inflation.

## Common traps

- Quoting nominal growth as 'economic growth' — always use **real** GDP for growth comparisons.
- Forgetting that in the base year the deflator is 100 by definition.
- Confusing the deflator with CPI/WPI: CPI and WPI use a **fixed basket**, while the deflator covers the **whole economy** and updates its weights automatically.

## Don't confuse

**Deflator vs CPI:** both measure inflation, but CPI tracks a fixed consumer basket while the GDP deflator reflects every item in GDP, including investment and government goods.

### In short

**The story in brief.** The background, the cause-and-effect and every term used are explained in the sections above; the essential facts to carry into the exam are these.

**TL;DR**

- Nominal GDP uses current prices; Real GDP uses constant base-year prices.
- GDP Deflator = (Nominal GDP ÷ Real GDP) × 100; it is 100 in the base year.
- The deflator is the most comprehensive price index — covers all goods/services in GDP, unlike fixed-basket CPI/WPI.
- Real GDP growth is the true measure of economic growth.
- Worked case: nominal 1320, real 1100 gives deflator 120 and real growth 10%.
keyPoints: Nominal GDP uses current prices; Real GDP uses constant base-year prices.
GDP Deflator = (Nominal GDP ÷ Real GDP) × 100; it is 100 in the base year.
The deflator is the most comprehensive price index — covers all goods/services in GDP, unlike fixed-basket CPI/WPI.
Real GDP growth is the true measure of economic growth.
Worked case: nominal 1320, real 1100 gives deflator 120 and real growth 10%.
items.mnemonic: Deflator = Nominal over Real times 100 — 'how much of nominal is just prices'.

items.title: Three Methods of Calculating National Income
items.body:
**In one line:** Output, income and expenditure are three faces of the same money circulating in the economy, so national income can be measured by adding up value added, or incomes earned, or spending — and all three give the same total.

**Why it is asked:** The three methods and the mistakes that break them (double counting, transfer payments, forgetting imports) are a favourite objective-question theme.

## Why the three methods agree

Every rupee of output is sold, so it becomes someone's **income**, and that income is eventually **spent**. This 'circular flow' means the three totals must match when measured correctly.

### 1. Product / Value-Added Method (output side)

- **Value added** = Gross Value of Output − **Intermediate Consumption** (the inputs bought from other firms).
- Add up value added across the **primary, secondary and tertiary** sectors to get **GDP at factor cost**.
- Using only value added (or only final goods) avoids **double counting** — counting the same item once as an input and again as output.
- **Worked example:** a farmer grows crops worth ₹1,000 using ₹300 of seeds and fertiliser. Value added = 1,000 − 300 = **₹700**. If the miller then turns the grain into flour worth ₹1,400, the miller's value added is 1,400 − 1,000 = ₹400 — never count the full ₹1,400 on top of the ₹1,000.

### 2. Income Method (income side)

- Add all **factor incomes** earned in production: **Wages + Rent + Interest + Profits + Mixed Income** (mixed income is the earnings of the self-employed, where wage and profit cannot be separated).
- **Transfer payments** (pensions, scholarships, subsidies) are **excluded** — they are not payment for current production.

### 3. Expenditure Method (spending side)

- **GDP at market price = C + I + G + (X − M)**: private **C**onsumption, **I**nvestment (gross capital formation, including the change in inventories), **G**overnment spending, and net exports (eXports − iMports).
- A **closed economy** has no foreign trade (X = M = 0) and no NFIA, so **GDP = GNP**; an **open economy** trades with the rest of the world.
- With no government and a closed economy, the identity reduces to **Investment = Savings (I = S)**.
- **Net exports (X − M)** include **invisibles** — services such as tourism, software and shipping. A foreign tourist's spending in India is an **export of services** (a credit in the accounts).

## Worked example (exam level)

For an economy (₹ crore): C = 600, I = 150, G = 200, X = 100, M = 50.
- GDP at market price = C + I + G + (X − M) = 600 + 150 + 200 + (100 − 50) = **₹1,000 crore**.
- A common slip is to add imports (M); imports are **subtracted**, because they are not produced at home.

## Common traps

- Double counting intermediate goods — count value added or final goods only.
- Including transfer payments in the income method.
- Forgetting to subtract imports (M) in the expenditure method.

## Exam shortcut

If a question lists C, I, G, X and M, it wants the **expenditure method** — just compute C + I + G + X − M. This shortcut does **not** apply when the data are factor incomes (wages, rent, interest) — then use the income method.

### In short

**The story in brief.** The background, the cause-and-effect and every term used are explained in the sections above; the essential facts to carry into the exam are these.

**TL;DR**

- Product method: GDP at FC = sum of (Gross Value of Output − Intermediate Consumption).
- Income method: NI = Wages + Rent + Interest + Profits + Mixed Income; transfer payments excluded.
- Expenditure method: GDP at MP = C + I + G + (X − M).
- All three methods give the same figure; only final goods/value added counted to avoid double counting.
- Closed economy without government: Investment = Savings (I = S).
- Closed economy: no foreign trade, X = M = 0, GDP = GNP; foreign tourists' spending in India = export of services (invisibles).
keyPoints: Product method: GDP at FC = sum of (Gross Value of Output − Intermediate Consumption).
Income method: NI = Wages + Rent + Interest + Profits + Mixed Income; transfer payments excluded.
Expenditure method: GDP at MP = C + I + G + (X − M).

items.title: Gross Value Added (GVA) and its link to GDP
items.body:
**In one line:** Gross Value Added is the value a producer or sector adds after subtracting the inputs it bought, and GDP is simply GVA plus the net taxes the government adds on products.

**Why it is asked:** Since 2015 India headlines GVA alongside GDP, sectoral growth is reported in GVA terms, and MCQs test the exact GVA-to-GDP bridge and the price concept each uses.

## What the terms mean

- **GVA (Gross Value Added)** = value of output − value of intermediate inputs. It is measured at **basic prices** (the price a producer receives before taxes on the product, but after any production subsidy).
- **Product taxes** = taxes charged per unit of a product (for example GST, excise); **product subsidies** = per-unit subsidies on a product.
- **Market price** = what the buyer finally pays, which includes product taxes.

## The GVA to GDP bridge

**GDP at market price = GVA at basic prices + Product Taxes − Product Subsidies.**

- GVA (basic prices) is the **supply/producer side**; GDP (market price) is the **demand side** at the prices buyers pay.
- Economists watch GVA because it strips out swings in tax and subsidy rates, giving a cleaner read of **real productive activity** by sector (agriculture, industry, services).

## How to convert (steps)

1. Start with GVA at basic prices.
2. Add product taxes collected on those products.
3. Subtract product subsidies given on them.
4. The result is GDP at market price.

## Worked example 1 (easy)

GVA at basic prices = ₹180 crore, product taxes = ₹25 crore, product subsidies = ₹5 crore.
- GDP at market price = 180 + 25 − 5 = **₹200 crore**.

## Worked example 2 (exam level)

Suppose GDP at market price = ₹200 crore and the government then **cuts** product subsidies by ₹5 crore (now ₹0) while GVA is unchanged at ₹180 crore and taxes stay ₹25 crore.
- New GDP = 180 + 25 − 0 = **₹205 crore**. GDP rose even though real production (GVA) did not — the gap came only from lower net subsidies. This is why a GVA-GDP growth gap signals changing net indirect taxes, not changing output.

## Common traps

- Adding subsidies instead of subtracting them in the bridge.
- Treating GVA and GDP as identical — they differ by net product taxes.
- Forgetting that GVA uses basic prices while GDP uses market prices.

## Don't confuse

**GVA vs GDP:** GVA answers 'how much did producers add?'; GDP answers 'what is output worth at the prices buyers pay?'. The difference is product taxes minus product subsidies.

### In short

**The story in brief.** The background, the cause-and-effect and every term used are explained in the sections above; the essential facts to carry into the exam are these.

**TL;DR**

- GVA = Output − Intermediate Consumption; measured at basic prices.
- GDP at market price = GVA at basic prices + Product Taxes − Product Subsidies.
- GVA is the supply/producer-side measure; GDP is the demand-side, market-price measure.
- India began publishing GVA prominently with the 2015 (base 2011-12) national-accounts revision.
- Sectoral growth (agri/industry/services) is analysed in GVA terms.
- A GVA-GDP growth gap reflects changing net product taxes, not changing real output.
keyPoints: GVA = Output − Intermediate Consumption; measured at basic prices.
GDP at market price = GVA at basic prices + Product Taxes − Product Subsidies.

items.mnemonic: GDP = GVA + (product taxes − subsidies): market price sits above basic price by net product taxes.

items.title: Base Year, the 2022-23 New Series & Statistical Agencies
items.body:
**In one line:** The base year is the fixed reference year whose prices are used to compute real GDP, and India has just moved that reference from 2011-12 to a new 2022-23 series compiled by the government's statistics office.

**Why it is asked:** The base year is current-affairs-sensitive (it changed in 2026) and the agencies and historical 'firsts' of national-income estimation are standard factual MCQ fodder.

## What a base year is

A **base year** is the reference year whose constant prices are used to measure **real** GDP. It is revised periodically so the price structure and the list of goods reflect the economy as it is today, not decades ago.

- **Earlier base year: 2011-12**, adopted in the **January 2015** revision, which also brought GVA at basic prices to the fore.
- **Current base year: 2022-23**, with the new series released on **27 February 2026**. MoSPI's **National Statistical Office (NSO)** revised the base to 2022-23, guided by the **Advisory Committee on National Accounts Statistics (ACNAS)** chaired by **Prof. Biswanath Goldar**. The new series uses newer data sources such as **GST, MCA-21 corporate filings and PLFS**. The Second Advance Estimates released with it put FY2025-26 real GDP growth at **7.6%**.

## Who compiles the data

| Body | Role |
|---|---|
| MoSPI (Ministry of Statistics & Programme Implementation) | Nodal ministry for official statistics |
| NSO (National Statistical Office) | Prepares national accounts and releases GDP estimates; formed in 2019 by merging the CSO and NSSO |
| NSC (National Statistical Commission) | Apex advisory body for statistics; set up in 2005 on the Rangarajan Commission's recommendation |

## Historical firsts

| Milestone | Who / when |
|---|---|
| First estimate of India's national income | Dadabhai Naoroji, in Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (1867-68) |
| First scientific estimate | V.K.R.V. Rao (1931) |
| First official post-independence body | National Income Committee (1949), chaired by P.C. Mahalanobis |

The National Income Committee's work led to setting up the **CSO (Central Statistical Office) in 1951**; its members included V.K.R.V. Rao and D.R. Gadgil.

## Why estimation is difficult

- A large **informal/unorganised sector** that keeps few records, which makes reliable data hard to collect.
- **Non-monetised** transactions — barter and goods households produce and consume themselves (self-consumption of farm produce), which are difficult to value because no price is paid.
- The **black economy** and weak data on small producers.

## Common trap

The base year is **not** the current year — in 2026 the latest base year is 2022-23, not 2025-26. And Naoroji made the **first** estimate, but V.K.R.V. Rao made the first **scientific** one — questions often swap these two.

### In short

**The story in brief.** The background, the cause-and-effect and every term used are explained in the sections above; the essential facts to carry into the exam are these.

**TL;DR**

- Current base year = 2022-23 (new series released 27 Feb 2026); replaced 2011-12 (adopted Jan 2015).
- 2022-23 new GDP series (released 27 Feb 2026) guided by ACNAS (chaired by Biswanath Goldar), NSO-MoSPI; uses GST, MCA-21, PLFS.
- NSO (CSO + NSSO merged in 2019) under MoSPI compiles national accounts; NSC (2005, Rangarajan) is apex advisory body.
- First national-income estimate: Dadabhai Naoroji (1867-68); first scientific estimate: V.K.R.V. Rao (1931).
- National Income Committee (1949) chaired by P.C. Mahalanobis was the first official post-independence NI body; led to CSO (1951).
- Estimation is hard due to the informal sector, non-monetised/self-consumption output and the black economy.

items.title: Market Price ↔ Factor Cost & Key Conversion Formulae
items.body:
**In one line:** Market price is what a buyer pays, factor cost is what producers actually earn, and you move between them by removing indirect taxes and adding back subsidies.

**Why it is asked:** Almost every national-income numerical hinges on applying the three conversions (price basis, gross/net, domestic/national) in the right order; one wrong sign changes the answer.

## What the terms mean

- **Market price** includes **indirect taxes** (such as GST) that the buyer pays to the government.
- **Factor cost** is the price after removing those taxes and adding back any **subsidies** — it is the income left for the factors of production (land, labour, capital, enterprise).
- **Net indirect taxes** = indirect taxes − subsidies.

## The conversions

**1. Market Price to Factor Cost:** Factor Cost = Market Price − Indirect Taxes + Subsidies.

**2. Gross to Net:** subtract **Depreciation**. **3. Domestic to National:** add **NFIA**.

## Formula ladder

| Step | Formula |
|---|---|
| GDP at Factor Cost | Sum of value added by all sectors |
| GNP | GDP + Net Factor Income from Abroad (NFIA) |
| NNP | GNP − Depreciation |
| National Income | NNP at Factor Cost = NNP at Market Price − Indirect Taxes + Subsidies |

## How to do it (steps)

1. Fix the price basis: to go from market price to factor cost, subtract indirect taxes and add subsidies.
2. Fix gross/net: subtract depreciation for a 'Net' figure.
3. Fix domestic/national: add NFIA for a 'National' figure.

## Worked example 1 (easy)

GDP at market price = ₹100 crore, indirect taxes = ₹10 crore, subsidies = ₹3 crore.
- GDP at factor cost = 100 − 10 + 3 = **₹93 crore**.

## Worked example 2 (exam level)

Given (₹ crore): GDP at market price = 100, NFIA = +5, Depreciation = 8, Indirect Taxes = 10, Subsidies = 3. Find National Income.
- GNP at market price = 100 + 5 = **105**.
- NNP at market price = 105 − 8 = **97**.
- National Income = NNP at factor cost = 97 − 10 + 3 = **₹90 crore**.

## Common traps

- Reversing the signs: it is **minus taxes, plus subsidies** for factor cost.
- A positive NFIA makes GNP greater than GDP; a negative NFIA (India's usual case, because payments to foreign investors exceed Indians' foreign earnings) makes GNP less than GDP.
- Mixing the order — but note the three conversions are independent, so the final answer is the same whatever order you apply them in.

### In short

**The story in brief.** The background, the cause-and-effect and every term used are explained in the sections above; the essential facts to carry into the exam are these.

**TL;DR**

- Factor Cost = Market Price − Indirect Taxes + Subsidies.
- GNP = GDP + NFIA; NNP = GNP − Depreciation.
- National Income = NNP at Factor Cost = NNP(MP) − Indirect Taxes + Subsidies.
- Positive NFIA means GNP above GDP; India's NFIA is usually negative, so GNP is below GDP.
- Worked case: GDP(MP) 100, NFIA +5, Dep 8, IT 10, Sub 3 gives NI = 90.
keyPoints: Factor Cost = Market Price − Indirect Taxes + Subsidies.
GNP = GDP + NFIA; NNP = GNP − Depreciation.

Positive NFIA means GNP above GDP; India's NFIA is usually negative, so GNP is below GDP.

items.mnemonic: MP to FC: 'minus taxes, plus subsidies' (taxes inflate market price, subsidies deflate it).

items.title: National Income — Building Blocks, Uses & Limitations of GDP
items.body:
**In one line:** national income is a flow of final output measured over a year inside a defined economic territory, and while it is the best single gauge of an economy's size, GDP misses unpaid work, inequality, the environment and the shadow economy.

**Why it is asked:** UPSC 2013 asked what national income "is equal to"; NCERT terms (flow, final vs intermediate, economic territory, normal resident) and the "limitations of GDP" list are standard one-liners.

## Building blocks (NCERT terms)

**The story**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **National income** | The **money value of all final goods and services** produced in a country during a year (UPSC 2013 key) |
| **Flow concept** | National income is a **flow** — measured **per period** (a year) — unlike wealth or capital, which are **stocks** at a point of time |
| **Final vs intermediate goods** | A good is **final** if bought for consumption or investment; **intermediate** if bought for resale or further processing in the same year. The **same good** (milk) can be either, depending on its **use** |
| **Economic (domestic) territory** | Includes the country's political frontiers plus its **embassies abroad** and **ships and aircraft** operated by residents; **excludes** foreign embassies in India |
| **Normal resident** | A person or institution whose centre of economic interest lies in the country (usually living there for a year or more) |
| **Depreciation** | **Consumption of fixed capital** — the wear and tear of capital goods during the year |
| **Value of output** | Sales + change in stock (inventories) |

## GDP vs GNP — the source's comparison

| Point | GDP | GNP |
|---|---|---|
| Basis | **Geographical boundary** | **Citizenship / nationality** |
| Foreigners' income earned in India | **Included** | Excluded |
| Indians' income earned abroad | Excluded | **Included** |
| Example | A factory in India run by a foreign company counts in India's GDP | An Indian company's income abroad counts in India's GNP |

## Uses of national income data

- **Economic policy-making** (framing monetary and fiscal policy).
- **Living standards** — it gives **per capita income** (national income ÷ population).
- **International comparisons** of economic performance.
- Macroeconomics, which studies these aggregates, is also called the **"Theory of Income and Employment"**.

## Limitations of GDP (as a welfare measure)

| Limitation | What GDP misses |
|---|---|
| **Non-market transactions** | **Unpaid domestic work** and volunteer services |
| **Quality of life** | Income **inequality**, happiness, well-being |
| **Environmental costs** | **Environmental degradation** and depletion of natural resources |
| **Shadow economy** | Informal / **black economy** activity |
| **Non-economic factors** | Health, education, political freedom |
| **Sustainability** | Whether growth is sustainable over the long term |

## Growth rate formula

**GDP growth rate = (GDP this year − GDP last year) ÷ GDP last year × 100.** Use real GDP for "economic growth".

## Don't confuse

- **Flow** (national income, per year) vs **stock** (capital, wealth, at a date).
- GDP counts **foreigners' production in India**; GNP counts **Indians' production abroad**.

**TL;DR**
- National income = money value of final goods and services produced in a year (UPSC 2013); it is a flow.
- The same good can be final or intermediate depending on its use.
- Economic territory includes Indian embassies abroad and resident-operated ships/aircraft; excludes foreign embassies in India.
- GDP misses unpaid domestic work, inequality, environmental degradation and the black economy.
- Growth rate = (this year − last year) ÷ last year × 100.
keyPoints: National income = money value of all final goods and services produced in a country during a year (UPSC 2013).
National income is a flow (measured per year); capital and wealth are stocks.
The same good can be final or intermediate depending on its use.
Economic territory includes the country's embassies abroad and ships/aircraft operated by residents; it excludes foreign embassies located in the country.
GDP is based on the geographical boundary; GNP on citizenship/nationality.
Limitations of GDP: misses unpaid domestic work, inequality, environmental degradation, the black economy and sustainability.
Macroeconomics is also called the "Theory of Income and Employment".
GDP growth rate = (GDP this year − GDP last year) ÷ GDP last year × 100.

items.title: The Three Methods — Factor Pairs, Identities & Worked Sums
items.body:
**In one line:** each factor of production earns a matching income, the expenditure method adds four kinds of final spending, and the circular-flow identities link saving, investment, the budget and trade.

**Why it is asked:** income-method pairings, "what is excluded", and the savings-investment identity appear as statement and assertion-reason questions.

## Income method — who earns what

**The story**

| Factor of production | Its income |
|---|---|
| **Labour** | **Wages and salaries** |
| **Land** | **Rent** |
| **Capital** | **Interest** |
| **Entrepreneur** | **Profit** |
| **Self-employed** (small traders, farmers) | **Mixed income** — wage and profit cannot be separated |

- Only **factor incomes** from production count; **transfer payments** (pensions, scholarships) are **excluded**.
- Worked sum (source): wages ₹10,000 + rent ₹5,000 + interest ₹3,000 + profits ₹2,000 = **₹20,000**.
- The income method is useful for analysing the **distribution of income** among factors.

## Production (value-added) method

- **GDP at factor cost = Σ (Gross Value of Output − Intermediate Consumption)**.
- The economy is divided into **primary, secondary and tertiary** sectors; this method shows each sector's **contribution**.
- Worked sum: crops worth ₹1,000 using ₹300 of seeds and fertilizers → value added **₹700**.
- Two sectors: agriculture (₹1,000 − ₹300) + industry (₹1,500 − ₹600) = combined GVA **₹1,600**.

## Expenditure method

- **GDP at market prices = C + I + G + (X − M)** — private consumption, investment (**gross domestic capital formation, including inventory investment**), government expenditure and net exports.
- Exports are **added** (foreigners' spending on our goods); imports are **subtracted** (spending on foreign goods).
- Worked sum (source): C ₹50,000 + G ₹10,000 + I ₹20,000 + net exports ₹5,000 = **₹85,000**.

## Circular-flow identities

- Households use income for **consumption, saving or taxes**: **GDP = C + S + T**.
- Setting C + I + G + X − M = C + S + T gives **(I − S) + (G − T) = M − X**: a private investment-saving gap plus a budget gap must be matched by a trade gap.
- With **no government and no foreign sector**, G = T = X = M = 0, so **I = S** (investment equals saving).
- **Indirect taxes** such as **GST** are added to factor cost to get market price; subsidies are subtracted.

## Don't confuse

- **Rent** goes to **land**, **interest** to **capital** — examiners swap them.
- **Mixed income** (self-employed) is included; **transfer payments** are not.

**TL;DR**
- Labour–wages, land–rent, capital–interest, entrepreneur–profit, self-employed–mixed income.
- Income example: 10,000 + 5,000 + 3,000 + 2,000 = ₹20,000; expenditure example: ₹85,000.
- Investment in the expenditure method includes inventory investment.
- GDP = C + S + T; (I − S) + (G − T) = M − X; with no government or trade, I = S.
keyPoints: Labour earns wages, land earns rent, capital earns interest, the entrepreneur earns profit; the self-employed earn mixed income.
Income-method example: wages ₹10,000 + rent ₹5,000 + interest ₹3,000 + profits ₹2,000 = ₹20,000.
Expenditure-method example: C ₹50,000 + G ₹10,000 + I ₹20,000 + net exports ₹5,000 = GDP ₹85,000.
Investment (I) is gross domestic capital formation, including inventory investment.
GDP = C + S + T, so (I − S) + (G − T) = M − X.
Indirect taxes such as GST are added to factor cost to get market price.

items.title: Base-Year Series, Price Concepts & Recent Estimates
items.body:
**In one line:** India has rebased its national accounts many times — from 1948-49 to 2011-12 and now 2022-23 — and since 2015 reports GVA at basic prices, a price concept sitting between factor cost and market price.

**Why it is asked:** "current base year", "headline metric since 2015" and the deflator's coverage are recurring factual items; recent growth numbers are current affairs.

## Base years of India's national accounts (CSO/NSO series)

**The story**

| Series | Base year |
|---|---|
| First official series (CSO) | **1948-49** |
| Later revisions | 1960-61, 1970-71, 1980-81, 1993-94, **1999-2000**, **2004-05** |
| Series adopted in January 2015 | **2011-12** |
| New series (released February 2026) | **2022-23** |

- The UN recommends revising the base year about every **five** years so that prices and the basket stay current.

## Three price concepts for value added

| Concept | How it relates |
|---|---|
| **GVA at factor cost** | Payments to factors only |
| **GVA at basic prices** | GVA at factor cost **+ production taxes − production subsidies** (taxes not tied to a unit of output, such as land revenue, stamp duty) |
| **GDP at market prices** | GVA at basic prices **+ product taxes − product subsidies** (taxes per unit, such as GST, excise) |

- Since the **2015 (base 2011-12)** revision, **GVA at basic prices** replaced GDP at factor cost as the headline sectoral measure.

## Deflator coverage

- **Nominal GDP** is calculated at current market prices and is not adjusted for inflation; **real GDP** uses constant base-year prices, and in the base year nominal = real.
- National accounts are compiled by the **NSO (MoSPI)**, not by the **RBI**.
- The **GDP deflator** covers **all goods and services produced domestically**, so — unlike the CPI — it **does not include the prices of imported goods**.

## State income (AP angle)

- Andhra Pradesh's **per-capita GSDP** in 2024-25 was **₹2,98,058**, above India's per capita income of **₹2,34,859**.
- AP's GSDP: **₹15.91 lakh crore** (2024-25 actuals) → **₹17.62 lakh crore** (2025-26 revised) → **₹19.75 lakh crore** (2026-27 projected).
- Each state's **GSDP** (Gross State Domestic Product) is estimated by its **Directorate of Economics and Statistics (DES)** using the national methodology; **Andhra Pradesh's** GSDP for 2026-27 is projected at about **₹19.75 lakh crore** (current prices).

## Recent estimates

- Real GDP growth **2025-26: ~7.6%** (new 2022-23 series).
- Real GDP growth **Q1 2026-27 (April–June 2026): 7.8%**.
- In **October 2026** the **IMF** said India's revised GDP methodology was consistent with international standards.

## Don't confuse

- **Production taxes** (bridge factor cost → basic prices) vs **product taxes** (bridge basic prices → market prices).
- **Firsts:** Dadabhai Naoroji's first estimate (1867-68) put India's per capita income at about **₹20** a year.
- **2011-12** = base adopted in **2015**; **2022-23** = base adopted in **2026**.

**TL;DR**
- Base years: 1948-49 (first) … 1999-2000, 2004-05, 2011-12 (Jan 2015), 2022-23 (Feb 2026).
- GVA at basic prices = GVA at factor cost + production taxes − production subsidies.
- GDP at market prices = GVA at basic prices + product taxes − product subsidies.
- The GDP deflator excludes the prices of imported goods.
- Growth: ~7.6% in 2025-26; 7.8% in Q1 2026-27.
keyPoints: India's first official national-income series had the base year 1948-49; later bases include 1999-2000, 2004-05, 2011-12 and 2022-23.
The UN recommends revising the base year about every five years.
GVA at basic prices = GVA at factor cost + production taxes − production subsidies.
GVA at basic prices became the headline sectoral measure with the 2015 (base 2011-12) revision.
The GDP deflator does not include the prices of imported goods (unlike the CPI).
Real GDP grew ~7.6% in 2025-26 and 7.8% in Q1 (April–June) 2026-27.
In October 2026 the IMF said India's revised GDP methodology was consistent with international standards.

items.title: National Income — Previous-Paper Traps
items.body:
**In one line:** previous papers test whether you know that nominal GDP almost always rises while real growth fluctuates, that a foreign tourist's spending is an export, and what a closed economy is.

**Why it is asked:** UPSC 2011, 2013 and 2015 built statement questions on exactly these points.

## The traps

**The story**

| Question theme | Correct idea |
|---|---|
| "GDP at market prices (in rupees) steadily increased over the decade" | **True** — nominal GDP rises almost every year because both output and prices rise (UPSC 2015) |
| "Real GDP growth rate steadily increased over the decade" | **False** — the real growth **rate** goes up and down (UPSC 2015, 2011) |
| "Per capita income growth steadily increased" | **False** — it also fluctuates (UPSC 2011) |
| Foreign visitors spending in India to watch a sporting event (Commonwealth Games 2010) | An **export** (of services) (UPSC 2011) |
| A "closed economy" | **Neither exports nor imports** take place; GDP = GNP (UPSC 2011) |
| National income equals | The **money value of final goods and services** produced (UPSC 2013) |

## Why the growth-rate trap works

- A **level** (GDP in rupees) can rise every year while its **growth rate** falls — e.g. GDP rising by 8% then 6% then 7% is still rising, but the rate is not "steadily increasing".

**TL;DR**
- Nominal GDP level rises steadily; real growth rate and per-capita growth fluctuate.
- Foreign tourists' spending in India = export of services.
- Closed economy = no exports, no imports.
keyPoints: GDP at market prices (current rupees) has risen steadily; the real GDP growth rate has not risen steadily (UPSC 2015).
Neither GDP growth nor per-capita income growth rose steadily in the five years before 2011 (UPSC 2011).
Spending by foreign visitors at the Commonwealth Games in India counted as an export (UPSC 2011).
A rising level of GDP is compatible with a falling growth rate.

items.title: For Mains — National Income
items.body:
National income is a Paper-IV (Economy & Development) staple: examiners rarely ask "define GDP" and instead probe measurement, reliability and whether GDP captures *development*. Organise the answer around the dimensions below.

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| **Concept & aggregates** | GDP → GNP (+NFIA) → NNP (−depreciation) → NI (NNP at factor cost); GVA at basic prices as the supply-side headline |
| **Measurement** | Product/value-added, income, expenditure methods converge on one figure (circular flow) |
| **Data reliability** | Informal sector (~45% of GVA), non-monetised output, black economy, base-year lags; IMF's 2025 low data-grade for India |
| **GDP vs welfare** | Ignores distribution, environment, unpaid work; need HDI, MPI, Gini, green accounting |
| **Reform / way forward** | New **2022-23 base-year series (27 Feb 2026)**; GST/MCA-21/PLFS integration; green & natural-capital accounting |

**Data points & authorities to quote:** new GDP series with base year **2022-23 released 27 Feb 2026** (replacing 2011-12), FY2025-26 real growth ~**7.6%**, GDP ~**₹322.6 lakh crore**; nominal GDP ~**$4.1 trillion** (3rd by PPP); services ~**54%**, industry ~**28%**, agriculture ~**18%** of GVA; **ACNAS (Prof. Biswanath Goldar)** guided the revision; **Dadabhai Naoroji (1867-68)** and **V.K.R.V. Rao (1931)** on the history; **National Income Committee 1949 (Mahalanobis)**; the Nobel-linked **Stiglitz-Sen-Fitoussi** critique of GDP-as-welfare.

**AP angle:** AP's **GSDP** rests on a large agrarian/fisheries and heavily informal base, so state-income estimation faces acute non-monetised-output and informal-sector gaps; AP is among states that have moved to the 2011-12 (and now 2022-23) GSVA framework and reports fast tertiary-sector growth around its services and construction activity.

**Use in answers:** (1) open by distinguishing *measuring output* from *measuring development*; (2) use a one-line **GDP → NI ladder diagram** to show command over concepts; (3) quote the **2022-23 base-year reform** as the "way forward" that modernises data sources; (4) close with the Stiglitz-Sen line that "what we measure shapes what we strive for" to argue for HDI/MPI/green-GDP supplements.
keyPoints: Frame answers as measurement + reliability + GDP-vs-welfare, not mere definitions.
New base-year series 2022-23 (released 27 Feb 2026) using GST/MCA-21/PLFS is the key 'way forward' point.
GDP ignores distribution, environment and unpaid work — cite HDI, MPI, Gini, green accounting.
Quote FY2025-26 real growth ~7.6%, GDP ~₹322.6 lakh crore, services ~54% of GVA.
AP angle: large informal/agrarian base makes GSDP estimation harder.
items.source: MoSPI/PIB — New GDP series base year 2022-23 (27 Feb 2026); Economic Survey 2025-26; Stiglitz-Sen-Fitoussi Report (2009)
